title: Garden City Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Garden City wells have a 44 ft median depth, with finished well costs modeled at $8,200-$15,100.
h1: Garden City, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or building near Garden City means looking closely at the well record before you price the property. Within five miles, Colorado DWR records list 3,477 permitted wells, with 2,140 recorded as constructed. The local pattern is unusually shallow: the median reported depth is 44 feet, and the middle half runs from 27 to 65 feet.

That does not guarantee the same result on a specific lot. The records include different uses, aquifers, construction dates, and reporting quality. Use them to set expectations, then confirm the neighboring wells, water rights, septic layout, and proposed building site before closing or drilling.

sections.heading: Garden City well depth is usually shallow
sections.html:
Garden City’s reported well depths are concentrated near the surface. Ninety-two percent are under 100 feet, while 7% fall between 100 and 300 feet and 1% fall between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 554 feet, so a shallow local median is not a promise for every parcel.

The 44-foot median, with the middle half from 27 to 65 feet, gives a driller a useful starting point for a bid. It also means a quote based on a much deeper hole deserves an explanation tied to the lot, target aquifer, casing, geology, or nearby well results. Permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers most often, followed by alluvial and Quaternary Alluvium records. Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 36% of the records.

sections.heading: Most Garden City wells report strong yields
sections.html:
Reported pumping results are favorable, but the yield data are limited to 321 wells. The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and 83% of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 16% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 2% are in the 1-to-5 range. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

For a buyer, the important distinction is between a reported test result and a guaranteed household supply. Ask for the completion report and pumping test for the specific well, including test duration and recovery. A domestic well still has a legal pumping limit of 35 gallons per minute for an exempt household-use well. Irrigation, stock, and other uses can involve different permit conditions.

sections.heading: Water levels are shallow in the current records
sections.html:
The median static water level is 16 feet below ground surface, with the middle half from 9 to 34 feet. That is a useful planning fact for pump setting, trenching, and septic layout, but static level is not the same as available well yield. Water can stand near the surface while the formation produces poorly, or pumping can lower the level around the well.

The decade series does not show a simple decline in the reported local data. The median measured level is 46 feet below surface for the 2010s and 15 feet for the 2020s. Those measurements may represent different locations, seasons, construction types, and aquifers, so do not treat the change as proof that the water table is rising everywhere. Compare nearby wells from La Salle, Evans, and Greeley only when their depths and aquifers are reasonably comparable.

sections.heading: Garden City’s permit history spans decades
sections.html:
Garden City has a long and continuing well record. Permits were issued in every decade from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year recorded as 2025. The busiest periods in the supplied records are the 1990s, with 501 permits, the 2010s, with 468, and the 2020s, with 492.

Records identify several recurring drillers. Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears most often, followed by Clement, Glenn A., and Lesh Drilling Inc. (Lesh Jr., Ed). A driller’s presence in the historical record does not establish current availability or performance on your parcel. Before relying on an old well, obtain the DWR permit, construction report, pump information, and current flow test. Confirm that the permitted use matches the house, livestock, irrigation, or proposed project.

sections.heading: What drilling can cost near Garden City
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 44-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $2,200 to $3,100. That is not the complete installation price.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,200 to $15,100 at that median depth. Actual bids can move outside that range because of access, casing and grout requirements, pump size, electrical distance, site conditions, water testing, and a deeper-than-expected hole. Ask for a written allowance for unsuccessful drilling, additional casing, surface restoration, and connections to the house. A shallow well can reduce drilling footage without eliminating the other parts of a functioning water system.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic, and dry-hole risk
sections.html:
Environmental screening deserves attention around Garden City. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 2,375 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 13 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mapped site is a reason to investigate, not proof that a particular well is contaminated. Test existing water for the contaminants relevant to the location and intended use, and review agency records before relying on an old test.

Low yield and a dry hole remain possible even where nearby records look strong. Confirm setbacks between the well, septic system, replacement leach area, property lines, and proposed building. Shallow water levels can complicate excavation and construction. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask a water attorney or engineer whether an augmentation plan is needed for the proposed use.

sections.heading: Before buying or building on a Garden City lot
sections.html:
Start with the nearest completed wells, not the countywide median. Compare their depth, aquifer name, permitted use, reported yield, static level, and construction date. La Salle, Evans, and Greeley are close reference areas, while Kersey, Gilcrest, and Eaton can provide broader context, but distance and geology still matter.

For an existing home, verify that the well serves the property legally and that the pump, pressure system, storage, electrical service, and water quality are functional. For vacant land, get a permit review before assuming a domestic well is available. Have the well location and septic reserve area staked against the house plan, driveway, and access route. Price the complete system, not just drilling, and make the purchase decision after reviewing the actual permit and test records.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Garden City, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Garden City is 44 feet. The middle half runs from 27 to 65 feet, and 92% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Some are much deeper: the deepest record is 554 feet. A nearby completed-well review is still necessary because aquifer, use, and location affect the result.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Garden City?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot for drilling in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 44-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $2,200 to $3,100. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,200 to $15,100. Access, casing, electrical distance, and added depth can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Garden City wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 321 local records that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. Eighty-three percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, and 16% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. These are reported results, not guarantees for a new well. Request the actual completion report and pumping test for the property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Garden City?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 2,375 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, along with EPA cleanup sites and historic mine features. That does not prove a specific well is affected. Test the property’s water using a laboratory and review environmental records before drinking or designing treatment.

faq.q: Do Garden City wells have a falling water table?
faq.a: The supplied decade data do not show a simple local decline. Median static water level was 46 feet below surface in the 2010s and 15 feet in the 2020s. Measurements can differ by location, season, aquifer, and well construction, so this comparison does not establish a rising or falling trend for every lot. Check nearby, comparable wells.
